title: Trump sues Iowa pollster over "wrong" 2024 Election poll

The November 2 survey placed Harris at forty-seven percent and Trump at forty-four percent. Trump ultimately won Iowa by approximately thirteen percentage points.
description_long:
Donald Trump sued Iowa pollster Ann Selzer, her firm, the Des Moines Register, and Gannett on December 17, 2024 over a poll showing Kamala Harris ahead before the election. The November 2 survey placed Harris at forty-seven percent and Trump at forty-four percent. Trump ultimately won Iowa by approximately thirteen percentage points.

The linked account says the lawsuit invoked Iowa's consumer fraud law and alleged that the survey deceived readers. The Register defended its work, releasing demographic information, cross-tabulations, technical explanations, and weighted and unweighted data. Its spokesperson rejected the lawsuit's merits. The source also describes media-law concerns that litigation of this kind could intimidate journalists.

A large polling error is not itself proof that results were knowingly fabricated. The event concerns the filing of allegations and the defendants' response, rather than an adjudicated fraud finding. title: Trump taps bank, Wall Street regulators for top posts

Jonathan McKernan was selected to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Jonathan Gould to head the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and Brian Quintenz to lead the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The selections involved agencies overseeing consumer finance, banking, and derivatives markets.
description_long:
Donald Trump announced several financial-regulatory nominations on February 11, 2025. Jonathan McKernan was selected to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Jonathan Gould to head the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and Brian Quintenz to lead the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The selections involved agencies overseeing consumer finance, banking, and derivatives markets.

The linked account also names John Hurley for Treasury's terrorism and financial crimes role and Brian Morrissey as Treasury general counsel. These backgrounds help explain the regulatory interests involved.

The nominations occurred amid efforts to curtail the CFPB's operations and growing attention to cryptocurrency oversight.
